name: Pattern 5: Early Warning, Then a Person Reaches Out
title: Pattern 5: Early Warning, Then a Person Reaches Out
answer: Pattern 5 is an early warning approach that combines attendance, grades, behavior records, and screening results to flag a student who may be slipping, then sends a person to reach out. It matters because the flag is not the intervention; the real work is a counselor, teacher, or attendance officer contacting the family and talking with the student to learn what is happening. The pattern also keeps human judgment at the end of the process, where bias and missed life events can be considered.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: The idea is to use existing school data to notice a student who is starting to slip before the problem becomes entrenched. Attendance, grades, behavior records, and screening results are combined into a flag that tells someone to look closer. The flag is only the beginning, because it does not explain why the student is struggling. A counselor, teacher, or attendance officer then calls the family, talks with the student, and works out what is really going on. This pattern solves the problem of unnoticed decline by turning data into a prompt for human contact rather than a final judgment.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the pattern begins with a flag built from attendance, grades, behavior records, and screening results, and then a staff member reaches out. The text does not set out separate steps for each grade band, but it does describe a trial in the early grades where personalized mailings told parents exactly how many days their child had missed. That early grade example shows how outreach can be direct and specific. The person who follows up may be a counselor, a teacher, or an attendance officer. Their job is to call the family, talk with the student, and find out what is really going on.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this area as having some of the strongest evidence in this Volume, and it notes that the evidence involves very little AI. In a large randomized trial, personalized mailings that told parents exactly how many days their child had missed cut chronic absence by 10 percent or more, largely because parents had underestimated the number (Rogers & Feller, 2018). A second trial in the early grades cut chronic absence by 15 percent (Robinson et al., 2018). Newer trials run by districts found smaller effects of around 2 percent, which is still real at low cost (Berger et al., 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out clear limits. Prediction models can carry bias, and people tend to read unclear results through the beliefs they already hold (Soland et al., 2020). Models also miss the events that actually push a student off course, such as a family move, a health problem, or a new job. That is why the pattern always ends with a person, who makes the call, has the conversation, and decides what to do next. Chapter 18 asks districts to publish the indicators they use so families can see what drives a flag.
